entities.name: Alexander, Count of Conversano
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alexander, Count of Conversano, was a significant Norman magnate in Apulia whose tumultuous career (c. 1110–1132) profoundly influenced the consolidation of Roger II's nascent Kingdom of Sicily. As the second count of Conversano, succeeding his father Geoffrey the Elder, Alexander initially inherited a powerful regional domain, but his persistent defiance against the unifying ambitions of Roger II placed him at the heart of the protracted Norman civil wars. His actions, often in league with other rebellious barons, represented a formidable challenge to the centralized authority Roger sought to impose across Southern Italy, delaying the full integration of Apulia into the new kingdom.

Alexander's tenure was marked by a series of armed conflicts and political maneuverings against Roger II, Duke of Apulia and Calabria, who later became King of Sicily. He participated in the major baronial revolt of 1127–1129, aligning with figures like Grimoald, Prince of Bari, and Tancred of Conversano. Following Roger's decisive victory at the Battle of Nocera in 1132, Alexander fled to Dalmatia, seeking refuge in the Byzantine Empire, and his county of Conversano was confiscated by the crown. His flight and the subsequent forfeiture of his lands were pivotal moments, demonstrating Roger II's resolve to crush independent baronial power and establish a unified, centralized Norman state in the Mezzogiorno.

The ultimate failure of Alexander and his allies to resist Roger II's ascendancy had a lasting impact, facilitating the rapid construction of the Kingdom of Sicily as a powerful Mediterranean entity. His defeat symbolized the end of an era of fragmented Norman lordships and the triumph of monarchical authority over feudal autonomy in Southern Italy. The confiscated lands of Conversano became a direct royal domain, strengthening the economic and territorial base of the new kingdom and setting a precedent for dealing with rebellious vassals.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Alexander's persistent but ultimately failed resistance against Roger II was a critical episode in the consolidation of the Kingdom of Sicily, illustrating the violent suppression of regional baronial power for centralized monarchical rule. His defeat led to the absorption of a major Norman county into the royal domain, strengthening the new kingdom's foundations.
